Kushanabha's Hundred Daughters

Stories of the Ramayana

Kushanabha's Hundred Daughters

The Story of a Hundred Daughters

In plain English — a story from Vishwamitra's own family

Stories by Eku

How to Read This Book · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it aloud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting with everyone at home.

In the yellow boxes, the characters speak in their own words. Change your voice a little as you read them — Vishwamitra grave, the daughters together, Vayu deep.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of each part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listener speak. This story is about patience and forgiveness — and thinking about patience is its real lesson.

This book is a story from Vishwamitra's own family. Rama and Lakshmana are on a journey, and their teacher tells them the story of his own ancestors — of a king who had a hundred daughters, and whose daughters did not give up their dharma even before a god.

The main story of this book comes from Valmiki's Ramayana, Balakanda, sargas 32–33. Where other traditions tell the tale a little differently, that is given separately at the end, under Where This Story Comes From — nothing has been mixed into the main story.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. He is travelling with his teacher Vishwamitra. In this story he is the listener.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. He is travelling with them too.

Vishwamitra — the great sage, teacher of Rama and Lakshmana. He is the one who tells this story — and it is the story of his own family.

Kusha — the son of Brahma, a great ascetic. Vishwamitra comes from his line.

Kushanabha — the son of Kusha, king of the city of Mahodaya, a righteous royal sage (rajarshi). His hundred daughters are the heroines of this story.

Ghritachi — Kushanabha's wife, a celestial maiden (apsara). The mother of the hundred daughters.

The hundred daughters — Kushanabha's hundred girls. Beautiful, well-mannered, dancing and singing, and holding their father's word as their dharma.

Vayu — the god of wind. He proposed marriage to the daughters, and, hearing their refusal, grew angry.

Brahmadatta — the son of the sage Chuli, a righteous king. Kushanabha married his hundred daughters to him — and by his touch the daughters were healed.

Gadhi — the son of Kushanabha, for whom the king performed a sacrifice. Gadhi's son is Vishwamitra.

1 · The Line of Kusha · · THE LINE OF KUSHA

The journey went on. Rama and Lakshmana were passing through a new land with their teacher Vishwamitra — a land ringed by five mountains and watered by the river Sona.

Rama asked — “Teacher, whose land is this? Which kings lived here?”

Vishwamitra smiled and said — “Rama, this land belongs to my own family. Listen, I shall tell you the story of my ancestors.”

“Long ago there lived a great ascetic named Kusha — the son of Brahma. Brahma gave him a boon that he would have four sons, and all four would found their own cities.”

“Kusha's wife was a princess of Vidarbha. From her were born four sons — Kushamba, Kushanabha, Adhurtarajasa and Vasu.”

“Kushamba founded the city of Kaushambi. Kushanabha founded the city of Mahodaya. Adhurtarajasa founded Dharmaranya. And Vasu built Girivraja — this very land we are walking on is Vasu's land, called Vasumati.”

Rama and Lakshmana looked all around — mountains, river, city, fields. Now the land felt even more their own — because it was the land of their teacher's ancestors.

Vishwamitra said: “Rama, now I shall tell you the story of Kushanabha — the dearest and the hardest story of my family.”

Pause and think — Vishwamitra said — this land belongs to my own family. Does hearing the story of our ancestors, knowing our roots, make a person stronger? Which story of your ancestors is dearest to you — and what does it teach you?

2 · The Hundred Daughters · · THE HUNDRED DAUGHTERS

In the city of Mahodaya ruled King Kushanabha — righteous, a royal sage, beloved of his people. His wife was Ghritachi — a celestial maiden, beautiful and gentle.

In their home were born a hundred daughters — a hundred girls. The story says they were as beautiful as streaks of lightning among clouds, like stars shining among the stars.

The hundred sisters grew up together — playing together, singing together, dancing together. The garden of Mahodaya echoed with their laughter.

They were not only beautiful — they were also well-mannered. Their father's word was their dharma. They used to say — our father is our master; he alone will decide our marriages.

One day they were playing in the garden — dancing, singing, picking flowers. Just then, passing by, came — Vayu, the god of wind.

Vayu saw the hundred daughters — their beauty, their laughter, their youth — and desire rose in his heart.

Pause and think — The hundred sisters played together, sang together — and what was their greatest strength? Their beauty — or their unity? When a hundred people stand together, of one mind, does their strength become a hundredfold?

3 · Vayu's Proposal · · VAYU'S PROPOSAL

Vayu came before the daughters and said —

Vayu said: “Maidens, I am Vayu — present in all things, going everywhere. Become my wives, all of you. The youth of humans lasts only a short time — marry me and you will stay young forever, become immortal, become goddesses.”

The hundred daughters looked at one another. Then they laughed — not at the proposal, but at the pride of one who, though a god, spoke to a man's daughters like this.

And then they answered together, in one voice —

The daughters said: “O Vayu, greatest among the gods! You pervade all things, we know your power — but why do you disgrace us so? We are the daughters of Kushanabha — and our father is our master. He alone will decide our marriages. By our penance we could displace even you from your place — but we will not, because we walk on the path of dharma.”

This answer was neither of anger nor of fear. It was an answer of dignity — we walk by our father's word, and no one, not even a god, can take our father's place.

Vayu heard this — and his anger flared up.

Pause and think — The daughters said — our father is our master. Is holding a father's word as dharma a weakness — or a strength? And when someone great, even a god, asks for something wrong, what does saying “no” show — fear, or courage?

4 · Vayu's Anger · · VAYU'S ANGER

Vayu's anger was like a storm arriving. He entered into the daughters' bodies — and twisted their limbs, bent them crooked.

In this book we will not look at that sight from close by — because what matters is not their pain, but the daughters' patience. Know only this — the hundred daughters became hunchbacked. Their backs bent, their limbs grew crooked, their beauty was hidden.

The daughters returned to the palace weeping, heads bowed in shame. Their tears flowed — but not one of them cursed Vayu, not one of them asked her father for revenge.

Kushanabha saw his hundred daughters — bent over, weeping, filled with shame — and his heart broke.

Kushanabha said: “Daughters, do not weep. What happened was a test of your patience — and you have passed it.”

The king heard the whole story from his daughters — Vayu's proposal, their refusal, and Vayu's anger. Hearing it, the king did not grow angry — he filled with pride.

Pause and think — The daughters became hunchbacked — but they did not curse Vayu, they did not ask for revenge. Is cursing and asking for revenge the only justice — or can patience and forgiveness also be justice? When something wrong happens to you, what do you do — curse, or stay patient?

5 · The Father's Answer · · THE FATHER'S ANSWER

Kushanabha called his daughters to him. The hundred daughters sat at their father's feet, heads bowed.

The king said —

Kushanabha said: “Daughters, what you did is very great. You turned down the proposal of a god — but you did not give up your dharma. You did not answer anger with anger — you answered with patience and forgiveness. That is your greatest strength.”

“You did not curse Vayu, though you could have. You did not ask for revenge, though you could have. You said — our father is our master. And today I say — all of you are my greatest treasure.”

The daughters' tears stopped. A father's pride was their greatest comfort.

Then Kushanabha thought — to whom shall I now marry these hundred daughters? Who is a groom who will accept a hundred daughters together — and by whose touch their suffering will be healed?

The king called his ministers, asked the sages — and then he found a name — Brahmadatta.

Brahmadatta was the son of the sage Chuli — righteous, radiant, and born by the blessing of Brahma. He was a king of whom it was said that his very touch heals suffering.

Pause and think — Kushanabha praised his daughters — their patience and forgiveness. Is a father's pride worth more than medicine for his daughters? When someone great takes pride in us, does our sorrow grow lighter?

6 · The Wedding and the Healing · · THE WEDDING AND THE HEALING

Kushanabha placed before Brahmadatta the proposal of marriage to his hundred daughters — and Brahmadatta accepted.

The wedding took place — the wedding of a hundred daughters, in a single pavilion, in a single blessed hour. And the moment Brahmadatta took the daughters' hands — a wonder happened.

(Slowly, with love) By his mere touch, the daughters' hunchbacks were gone. Their backs straightened, their limbs were healed, and they became as beautiful as before — shining even more brightly.

A festival was celebrated in the city of Mahodaya. Kushanabha said again and again, in joy — my daughters are freed from Vayu's hold!

And from that time the city of Mahodaya received a new name — Kanyakubja. Kanya — daughters; kubja — hunchbacked. The city where the hunchbacked daughters lived came to be called Kanyakubja — the city of the daughters.

But the story did not end here. One thing was still unfinished in Kushanabha's home — he had no son. The king performed a sacrifice for a son — and a son was born to him — Gadhi.

And Gadhi's son was — Vishwamitra. The same Vishwamitra who was at this moment telling this story to Rama and Lakshmana.

Vishwamitra said: “Rama, this is the story of my family. Kushanabha's hundred daughters — my own ancestors. Their patience, their forgiveness, their dharma — that is the identity of my family.”

Rama and Lakshmana bowed to their teacher. Now they knew — their teacher was not only a sage; he came from a family whose daughters had not given up their dharma even before a god.

The patience of a hundred daughters, the pride of one father —
and a wedding that made them all whole.

Pause and think — The daughters were healed — by Brahmadatta's touch. But were they healed only by that touch — or also by their patience, their father's pride, and their dharma? And why did Vishwamitra tell this story — did he want to give his disciples the identity of his family?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

This book is the story of a hundred daughters — and it teaches us three things.

First — unity. The hundred daughters answered together, in one voice. One daughter alone could have been frightened — a hundred could not. Unity was their greatest strength.

Second — patience and forgiveness. The daughters did not curse Vayu, they did not ask for revenge. They did not give up their dharma — and in the end that very patience freed them.

Third — a father's pride. Kushanabha did not blame his daughters, he did not shame them — he praised them. And that praise became their greatest medicine.

Ask the listeners:

1. The hundred daughters answered together — in one voice. Is standing together stronger than standing alone? Remember a moment like that from your own life.

2. The daughters said — our father is our master. Is holding a parent's word as dharma a weakness — or a strength?

3. The daughters became hunchbacked — but they did not curse. Is cursing the only justice — or can forgiveness also be justice?

4. Kushanabha praised his daughters, he did not blame them. When someone takes pride in us, how does our sorrow feel?

5. By Brahmadatta's touch the daughters were healed. Is healing only of the body — or also of the heart?

6. Vishwamitra told the story of his own family. Is knowing the story of our ancestors the same as knowing ourselves?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book comes from Valmiki's Ramayana, Balakanda, sargas 32–33 — in sarga 32, Kusha's four sons and their cities, Kushanabha's hundred daughters, Vayu's proposal, the daughters' refusal and Vayu's anger; in sarga 33, the daughters telling their father, Kushanabha's praise, the marriage to Brahmadatta and the daughters' healing by his touch.

Brahmadatta — Son of Chuli

Brahmadatta was the son of the sage Chuli — born by the blessing of Brahma, a righteous king. Kushanabha married his hundred daughters to him, and by the mere touch of his hand the daughters' hunchbacks were gone — that is what Valmiki says (Balakanda 33.23).

The Name Kanyakubja

The origin of the name Kanyakubja is told from this very story — kanya (daughters) + kubja (hunchbacked). The city where the hunchbacked daughters lived came to be called Kanyakubja — today's Kannauj. This is a traditional derivation, handed down from Valmiki's story.

Gadhi and the Kausiki River — Sarga 34

The birth of Kushanabha's son Gadhi and the story of the river Kausiki come in the next sarga, sarga 34. In this book Gadhi's birth is kept in brief, to complete the story, and its source is named separately here. Gadhi's son is Vishwamitra — which is why this is a story from Vishwamitra's own family.

The Daughters' Answer

The daughters had told Vayu — our father is our master, and by our penance we could displace even you from your place. In this book that answer is given in plain, dignified words — keeping the daughters' courage and dignity intact.

The Cities of the Four Brothers

Kusha's four sons founded four cities — Kushamba founded Kaushambi, Kushanabha founded Mahodaya, Adhurtarajasa founded Dharmaranya, and Vasu founded Girivraja. Vasu's land was called Vasumati — the same land from which Vishwamitra was telling this story.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of Kushanabha's hundred daughters comes to rest — but Rama's journey goes on. Ahead lies Siddhashrama, where the teacher's sacrifice is, and where Rama will fight demons for the first time. That story will be told in its own book.

And whenever you see a hundred people standing together, in one voice, remember the garden of Mahodaya — where a hundred sisters did not give up their dharma even before a god.

— The End —
